newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Greece press Albania on political talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Greece press Albania on political talks.

text.p: The United States has no plans to evacuate Americans from Albania and has not ordered a draw-down of its diplomatic staff there, the State Department said on Thursday.
"The U.S. ambassador (in Tirana) has not requested any kind of military assistance," spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
Burns said there were no plans for withdrawal of American diplomats from the country and "we're not planning right now an evacuation of American citizens."
U.S. military commanders stationed in Germany reported earlier on Thursday that they are developing plans to evacuate more than 1,600 Americans living in Albania.

Burns welcomed Albanian President Sali Berisha's decision to suspend military action against armed insurgents in the south and said the United States hoped this would open the door to a broader political settlement of the crisis there.

Earlier, the United States and Greece pressed Albania to open serious talks with the political opposition and Washington implored Berisha to receive a mission from the Organisation on Security and Cooperation (OSCE) trying to resolve the crisis.

At the start of talks at the State Department, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos expressed grave concern over the unrest in Albania sparked by the collapse of financial pyramid schemes.

"We know the situation in Albania is creating great concern for everyone," said Pangalos. He expressed particular worry about a potential influx of refugees that would overtax Greece's immigrant population of Albanian Greeks "which is very close to the tolerance (breaking) point."
Pangalos declined to dictate a solution to Albania's political problems but "the solution should include not only the government but all the political forces" in the country.
Albright also voiced concern, saying, "We believe it is highly important that there be a peaecful solution to the whole issue."
"We are very supportive of the OSCE mission that is going there" and will include an American representative, Representative Eliot Engel, a New York Democrat, she said.
In a television interview later, Albright commended Berisha's decision to suspend military action against the insurgents and called for a peaceful resolution.
"Military solutions never work," she said on the PBS programme "Newshour with Jim Lehrer." "President Berisha seems to have taken some positive steps today."
After the one-hour Albright-Pangalos meeting, Burns issued a strong U.S. call for Berisha to receive the OSCE mission, to be headed by former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky.
The 54-member OSCE, Europe's top security body, on Tuesday appointed Vranitzky to travel to Albania and assess the situation in the troubled nation.

Although the European Union also had a mission to Albania, the OSCE mission was even more critical because it has wider representation and was successful in December in pushing Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic toward compromise with politcal opponents, Burns told reporters.
"We call on President Berisha to receive Mr. Vranitzky as an emissary from OSCE and to engage in very serious talks with him," Burns said.

"We believe Berisha should put together talks with the opposition ... He needs to find a way to talk to them on a peaceful basis," he said, arguing that Berisha had "stiff(ed) the opposition" on talks, organised his own quick re-election as president, imposed a state of emergency and used miliary force against protestors.
Anger over the failed pyramid schemes has spread across Albania. At the weekend rioters burned and looted in the border region and stole thousands of arms from state arsenals.

But on Thursday, Berisha, backed by Albania's opposition parties, agreed to suspend military activity against rebels in the south and to offer an amnesty to insurgents who surrendered weapons within two days. The offer was made public in a statement after more than five hours of talks.
